about: `complexity` counts how much a statement says, and that count is preserved
when two statements are put together: what BOTH require plus what EITHER
accepts equals the sum of the parts. It is inclusion-exclusion, and it is
what makes the count a measure rather than an index.
On ideals the count conserves on every finite poset: the up-sets of any
poset form a distributive lattice. `isDistributive` still reports whether
the LEVEL view is faithful (a ladder). The falsifier that used to live
here is L0 — a non-closed pair is refused — and lives in ideals.json.
ON A LADDER THIS LAW IS TRIVIAL. For a total order the highest and lowest
of two levels are just those two levels again, so ANY weighting satisfies
it and nothing is being tested. The cases below that carry weight are the
ones off a ladder. M3 now conserves because the valuation counts excluded
levels of a declared Ω, not irreducibles.

coverage.criterion: a ladder (trivial), a distributive non-ladder (the real claim), and a non-distributive lattice on both measures (the falsifier)
coverage.why: three scales only; exhaustive checks over all pairs are asserted in the unit tests
coverage._note: size said 5 against three cases. The criterion names three and there are three, so the number was the typo — and it went unseen because the adequacy check iterated a hand-kept list of seventeen names while the directory held nineteen, and this file was one of the two it never read.

cases.name: a ladder is distributive, and the law holds trivially
the 2x2 powerset — distributive, and the claim is real here
the diamond M3 — a lattice, not distributive
